analytic.title: Leveraging Real-Time Network Analyses by Extending a Model-based Framework

div.p: Real-Time Systems are subject to temporal requirements. To check if these latter are met, performance analysis tests are required. However, the performance analysis through model-based process is still difficult due to (i) the complexity of real-time systems (ii) and the lack of methodologies enabling to leverage performance tests to be applied easily to design models.

In this paper, we focus on the temporal scheduling analysis of distributed systems with real-time networks. We present an extension of a pivot scheduling analysis aware methodology in order to explicit the analysis models. That is, we propose a modeling viewpoint dedicated to distributed real-time systems in order to bridge the semantic gap between system design and analysis techniques of real-time networks.

Our proposed extension has been implemented and integrated in a modeling framework dedicated to the schedulability analysis. The paper also contains a case study that stresses the contribution and shows its usefulness.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Hard real-time systems require to respect temporal constraints (e.g., deadline, end-to-end delay, processor utilization, etc.) in order to insure a sound execution of the whole system. Otherwise, an unexpected behavior or a catastrophic accident may occur. Validation of such systems requires to verify that temporal constraints will be met. That can impact sharply the time-to-market if the verification is executed late in the design process. Thus, it is primordial to apply reliable temporal analyses, at an early design stage.

div.head: A. Context
div.p: As the complexity of real-time systems increases in avionics as well in automotive systems, distributed systems help to overcome these problems by distributing tasks which communicate through real-time networks. In this paper, we focus on schedulability analysis tests to perform temporal analyses and especially those dedicated to real-time networks, like the worst-case response time (WCRT) and the worst-case transmission time (WCTT) of network messages. On the one hand, every scheduling test is based on an abstraction view (a.k.a. analysis model or workload model) of the system underdesign. Each view relies on a set of qualitative and quantitative timing information characterizing relevantly the worst-case behaviors of the system. On the other hand, analysis tests are based on algebraic equations using timing information from the abstraction view. Several tests have been implemented as simple prototypes and academic/commercial tool-suites which inputs deal with scheduling analysis abstraction views, but with formalisms that differ from one tool to another.

Recently, model-driven engineering (MDE) paradigm [1] has been widely used by academics and industrial practitioners [2] not only to design systems but also to apply temporal performance analyses during the design stage. Indeed, several modeling languages (such as UML MARTE [3], AADL [4] or EAST-ADL [5]) have been provided to "modeling architects" to embody functional components abstracting behaviors, communication mediums and execution platforms. We describe these standard design languages as "architecture-centric" since they provide concepts that are common to several analyses and further usage related to embedded systems (see Part (a) of Figure 1). Moreover, to check the temporal behavior correctness of system designs, "analysts", often apply analyses through a model-based tool-chain to conclude about the systems schedulability. However, this task (illustrated in Figure 1) is not easy and is still driven by the analysts experiences.

div.head: B. Problem Statement
div.p: Since the analysis tools inputs do not conform to the architecture-centric languages, model transformations have to be defined to "extract and derive" timing information required by the chosen analysis tool. This information differs from a system situation to another. Also, the result of an analysis test can never be reliable unless the system architecture fits accurately with the analysis model (i.e., the abstraction view) of the applied test. Another point is that analysis tests are scattered in different tools and there is no tool that provides all tests. Consequently, the modeling and the analysis of real-time systems through a model-based process require competences in both modeling and analysis domains, which is uncommon.

div.head: C. Work positioning and Contributions
div.p: In this research, we aim at helping real-time systems architects by proposing a model-based methodology describing explicitly the information, that has to be extracted from the design in order to be able to analyze the real-time network. The underlying idea behind our proposition is also to reduce the semantic gap and shortening the time between recent research advances and industrial engineering practices, by enabling architects to capitalize their analysis knowledge. Our proposition emphasizes real-time networks since it is an extension of our recent work [6]. The extension is implemented and integrated as a part of MoSaRT framework [7]. The objective is not to propose yet another design language, but to cover as much as possible the analysis models (even those their tests are not yet implemented or integrated in tools) proposed by the research community (see Part (b) of Figure 1). It is important to note that the concepts proposed in this paper to represent the networks could be included in other suitable domain specific languages.

div.head: D. Paper Outline
div.p: The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Section II is devoted to present real-time networks trends and to clarify our work positioning via a motivating example. While Section III presents the scientific approach followed to propose foundation concepts of our contribution, Section IV discusses the implementation. Section V tackles the modeling and analysis of a case study by using two network protocols. Finally, Section VI summarizes and concludes this paper.

div.head: A. Real-Time Network concerns
div.p: Critical real-time embedded systems are mostly hard-wired. In the following, we present real-time aspects of two main real-time network protocols for critical embedded systems presenting the main types of protocols in distributed systems, shared bus and an Ethernet related network. The first one is popular in automotive domain and the second one emerges in avionics.

A Controller Area Network (CAN) [8] bus may be shared between several nodes, which are allowed to send and receive messages once the network is available. The message identifier is used as a priority. Then, a node sending a message stops when it realizes that a message with a higher priority than its message priority is already sent on the bus. In a scheduling analysis point of view, the network behaves exactly like a nonpreemptive fixed-task priority scheduler [9].

A Local Interconnect Network (LIN) [10] is another type of shared bus. The protocol is based on a master -slave relationship. The master have to send orders and ask for answer to the slave component. The scheduling is made offline to determine the scheduling table for the network.

The AFDX (Avionics Full DupleX switched ethernet) network is the backbone of an Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) system, particularly used in airborne systems [11]. It uses Ethernet switches to transfer data from one node of the plane to another node, in order to connect local networks on the system. As an extension of the fairly old ARINC 429 protocol [12], its behaviour consists in allowing a source endsystem to send messages to several destination end-systems, through logical channels called Virtual Links (VL). The VLs have two temporal parameters usually required for dimensioning a network: the period between each frame called the Bandwidth Allocation Gap (BAG) and the length of a frame transiting the network with a known throughput. The endsystems then deliver and/or receive messages from their local network. The links, between end-systems and switches and between switches, are dedicated Ethernet cables. Therefore, there is no contention when accessing to a physical link, and the arbitration (i.e. scheduling) of messages occurs in the output buffers of the switches.

div.head: B. Discussion
div.p: Modeling embedded systems with real-time aspects is often done with UML-MARTE or AADL. The modeling on these languages focuses more on the system architecture than the temporal behavior. Actually, analyzing a model requires to do efforts to explicit the temporal analysis characteristics. Several works have been tried to combine modeling languages with analysis tools. For example, Tempo, which is a framework developed by Henia et al. [13], aims to join analysis and modeling. However, users of Tempo needs to know the test that matches their design before performing analysis (based on their experience). Then, users can construct manually a new model derived from the first one but adapted to be acceptable by the analysis tool(s) implementing the test. In [14], authors have also proposed to bridge the AADL-based modeling and analysis, however their approach is hard coded since is based on several simplistic design patterns that cannot be extended. This paper is derived from a work conducted via a project consortium with industrial partners. We realize that multiplying the meta-models with the analysis input models is time consuming (e.g. through training, changes in design). Thus, we poropose a single methodology with modular design concepts to overcome the differences between CAN and AFDX. This methodology has to enable an iterative design, to ease the reuse and the adaptation of design semantics to conduct analyses.

Moreover, the methodology we propose to analyze network is not accounted in existing design languages to the best of our knowledge. In the following, we present an example presenting some limits of architecture centric design languages. We present a motivating example by considering a simple real-time system in order to depict the difference between design and analysis models and to show its significance. The considered example is composed of two tasks, each one mapped to a process. The processes are themselves mapped to two different processors. The processors communicate through a CAN bus (see Figure 2). To analyze the schedulability of the system depicted in Figure 2 many analysis tools may be applied. For example, to analyze this system with MAST [15], the design has to be interpreted into specific inputs as shown in Table I. We notice that AADL enables to well design the architecture of the system, but only few scheduling analysis information can be directly extracted, like tasks, their periods, deadlines and priorities. Then, for CAN communications, there is no possibility to indicate messages length, priority, scheduler and periods (see dark row of Table I). A part of the timing information related to the message is derived from the task sending the message, and another part is related to the chosen network protocol. Actually, since modeling with AADL is design-oriented, the parameters are more related to the system execution architecture and the implementation (for code generation) than to the scheduling analysis. This gap between the design and the analysis model of the discussed example is often filled by the experience of modellers and analysts. Unfortunately, this experience is neither persisted 3. Principle of MoSaRT framework [7] nor capitalized, hence the idea behind MoSaRT framework which is dedicated to make analysis models explicit during the development life-cycle. Consequently, this paper proposes to develop an extension of MoSaRT in order to cover the scheduling analysis of real-time networks.

div.head: D. MoSaRT framework
div.p: MoSaRT framework is an existing model-based framework developed by Y. Ouhammou [7]. To ease the analysis process, MoSaRT connects real-time designs expressed in standard design languages to many scheduling analysis tools. A summary of the MoSaRT capabilities is sketched in Figure 3. On the one hand, the framework is composed of a pivot prescriptive language dedicated to express scheduling analysis models (see MoSaRT Design Language in Figure 3).

The pivot language serves as a common basis to conduct the analysis of systems. On the other hand, the framework provides a descriptive language dedicated to construct analysis repositories (see MoSaRT Analysis Repository in Figure 3). Every analysis repository plays the role of a decision support and helps designers to choose appropriate scheduling analyses that match the system under-analysis. Several model transformations are available from MoSaRT to various analysis tools. Moreover, the analysis results can be returned to the pivot model, or to the original model via the pivot model for further modifications and then launching again the process. The process here is analysis method driven, opposite to Tempo presented in previous sub-section. The tool associated to the analysis is then proposed by the framework.

div.head: III. CONTRIBUTION
div.p: This section is dedicated to expose our contribution. First, we present a set of the well-known tests that correspond to real-time network analysis in order to identify analysis models (real-time properties and concepts) needed by these tests.
Secondly, we elaborate a model as a viewpoint regrouping all the identified elements. It will be the entry-point to instantiate several analysis models bridging designs and tools.

div.head: A. Scientific process: foundation concepts of our proposition
div.p: Delays on a network must be assessed to avoid unexpected behavior on the system. So, several tests have been proposed to determine WCTT. This latter relies on the specificities of the used networks (as it is discussed in Section II-A).

For a CAN bus, Davis et al. proposed a Response Time Analysis (RTA) [9] to calculate WCTT on the network, since a message transmitted through a CAN network is considered as a non preemptible task. To conduct this analysis, several parameters are needed. In the following, we enumerate those related to messages:
• the minimum time interval between two frames,
• the transmission-time on the network, • the priority of the frame on the network, • the blocking time,
• the eventual jitter due to the message emission.

For AFDX networks, we focus on seminal analysis techniques. R. Cruz developed the network-calculus method based on Min-plus algebra [16]. The network-calculus method considers the topology of the network. Indeed, for each virtual link (VL), an arrival curve γ(t) can be established, corresponding to the quantity of bits the virtual link sent at time t. It can be calculated with the maximal size of a frame and the BAG (Bandwidth Allocation Gap). For each node, a service curve β(t) is calculated, i.e. the number of bits transmitted at time t. An upper bound on worst-case transmission time can be determined with these elements:
• the maximal length of a frame • the BAG: period between two consecutive frames,
• the throughput of the network,
• the virtual links that are going through each node.

Kemayo et al. proposed another method, called the Forward Analysis (FA) [17], that also requires the network topology. The method considers the latency suffered due to the emissions of the frames on an AFDX network. For each node crossed by the frame, the method evaluates the worst local delay suffered by the frame. The FA method requires the maximal delay needed to reach the destination node and the maximal pending workload on the node. This latter is the delay of the frames waiting to be transmitted at the arrival. This method computes the worst case delay on the network. That needs the following parameters.
• the maximal length of a frame • the BAG: period between two consecutive frames,
• the throughput of the network,
• the number of switches,
• the detailed path of each virtual link.

To analyze the end-to-end flows, it is necessary to consider the temporal behavior of each end, the temporal behavior of the network, and the impact generated to each-other until finding the stabilized worst-case behavior. Holistic analysis [18] is a method that can be considered to analyze the whole system. The method considers local delays in the origin processor and the destination processor. The analysis merges different analyses available on each section of the system, one for a processor, another one for the network, etc. It is then the worst-case end-to-end response time for a transaction given by the method with all system delays are accounted. Recently, a holistic analysis adapted to AFDX has been presented [19]. It takes into account the latency in end-systems and in switches to perform the upper bound of end-to-end delays.

div.head: B. Real-time network viewpoint
div.p: Referring to the study of section III-A, we aim to propose a generic meta-model for real-time networks presenting all characteristics of the systems. The modeling has to take into consideration the network topologies to be compatible with a large panoply of analysis tests such as Forward Analysis and Network calculus. In addition to the state of the art on real-time networks, we have also studied the inputs of many analysis tools [20], [15]. We notice that there are protocolindependent concepts (concepts which are common to most of the networks) and protocol-specific concepts (concepts dependent of the network protocol). The concepts are categorized as shown in Table II. The dark blue row represent the protocol-specific concepts and the light blue ones represent the protocol-independent concepts. These categorization of concepts inspire us to develop an analysis-oriented meta-model for real-time networks. To illustrate real-time network concepts, in this paper, we have chosen to extend the MoSaRT design language. Of course, this illustration can be implemented in different ways (like developing a new domain-specific language, extending AADL, MARTE or the formalism of a specific analysis tool).

Since the current version of MoSaRT meta-model allows a step-by-step development driven by the analysis, the extension must be compatible with such a development. Our aim is to propose an easy-to-use extension to comply with academic analysis input models. Such a model compliant with several analysis software implies a generic pivot meta-model. Nevertheless, the current version of MoSaRT meta-model provides minimalist concepts related to the real-time networks: the meta-model actually lacks of precision on the network topology, or at least not engough precision to approach the real behavior. The network can be modeled by instantiating a generic meta-class called HpCommunicationChannel, which does not contain advanced details. Thus, the compatibility with analyses presented in sub-section III-A is reduced. The lack of precision may increase the latency on the network and lead to a very pessimistic analysis referring to the system behavior in practical usages.

div.head: C. Extension of MoSaRT design language
div.p: The extension has to intend to refine the network representation on MoSaRT framework. Figure 4 presents the main aspects of our extension in hardware, software and "real-time properties" packages of the meta-model. Elements of Figure 4 are expressed in Ecore language [21] which is an UML-like class diagram [22]. Classes of hardware package are the ones which the name starts by "Hp" (for HardwarePlatform). Classes of software package are the ones which the name starts by "So" (for SoftwareOperators). Names of real-time properties package Elements start by "RTP" (for RealTimeProperties).

Initially, to specify a communication, the meta-model provided only the CommunicationChannel. After extension, the communication channel class is composed of HpNetworkNode, which is an abstract class that allows to specify the nodes of the network, like switches or ports of end-systems. While the switches can be defined by instantiating HpCommunicationSwitch class, ports of routers and end-systems can be represented by using HpCommunicationPort class. Moreover, switches and ports can be connected to each other by instantiating HpFlowCarrier. Thanks to the attributes of the HpCommunicationChannel class, the specification of the network protocol, the flow rate and the arbitrary policy can be made. All attributes complex types have been added to the RealTimeProperties package. Changing from a network protocol to another is simply a matter of a class reference. Real-time systems can be composed of several networks. Thus, HpCommunicationRouter is a class intended to connect between many networks. Common ports (instances of HpCommunicationPort) between channels and a router will then define the connected channels (as sub-networks) to the network. Besides, the software side shows that a task (instance of SoSchedulableResource) can either write or read a communication resource. In the case of a distributed system, the resource is a remote resource (instance of SoRemoteCommResource), which plays the role of a logical support of a message transmitted (SoTransmittedData) on the network. Indeed, an instance of SoRemoteCommResource represents a virtual connection between two tasks or more. It refers to, at least, a source task and one or more target tasks. By means of relationship between SoRemoteCommResource and HpFlowCarrier, we can define the route taken by messages.
Following this extension. We have noticed that a set of structural rules have to be satisfied during instantiating in order to get correct analysis models. These rules are listed hereafter.

• No-loop: target and origin switches of a HpFlow-Carrier shall be different. • Unique connection: a connection is represented by one and only one HpFlowCarrier. • Priority declaration: if a network needs to specify a priority on network frames (for example, CAN network), all SoRemoteCommResource connecting two tasks on the CAN bus must be declared on the network. • Unique sender task: if the declared network is an AFDX protocol, no more than one task can write on a Virtual Link.

• Full path: the path of a SoRemoteCommResource declared as a list of HpFlowCarrier shall link target tasks to the source task. The framework will take into account the referenced network in the class to adapt the proposed analysis and then to adapt the input model at the model to model transformation. As the framework is designed for temporal analysis, and with the knowledge of the analysis tools, only useful real-time parameters are retained in the meta-model at the transformation.

div.head: IV. TOOLING: IMPLEMENTATION OF THE CONTRIBUTION
div.p: This section is devoted to present software tools that have been used to implement our proposal. The implementation has been done at different levels: (1) the meta-model extension, (2) the structural rules and (3) the concrete syntax.

1) The implementation of the extended meta-model is based on EMF (Eclipse Modeling Framework [21]). 2) OCL (Object Constraint Language [23]) is used to implement rules, which we have been added after the extension to guarantee a coherent usage by checking the conformity of analysis models to MoSaRT meta-model.

3) The MoSaRT design language is a DSL (domain specific language), equipped with a graphical concrete syntax which facilitates its utilization through user-friendly editors. Then, we have also extended this syntax and we have updated all editors in order to cover all modifications related to the extension and enhance the useintuitive. Eclipse Sirius software [24] has been used for the concrete syntax extension. Finally, the extended MoSaRT design language can be used as a plug-in compliant with Eclipse tool [25].

div.head: V. CASE STUDY
div.p: This section proposes the modeling and analysis of a distributed system by using the extended MoSaRT framework. The case study will be analyzed with a CAN network and an AFDX network. First, we consider a distributed real-time network. The network protocol is unknown at this stage. This example is inspired from an example discussed by Grolleau et al. [26]. Figure 5 depicts the whole system. For instance, the figure shows that while τ 1 and τ 2 are executed on P rocessor A on which the scheduling policy is FPP (Fixed Priority Policy) and the priority of τ 1 is higher that τ 2 , the execution on P rocessor B is managed according to EDF (Earliest Deadline First). On P rocessor C , the scheduling policy is also FPP with τ 7 priority is higher than τ 9 priority, itself higher than τ 8 priority. More timing information is presented in Table III.

div.head: A. Modeling oriented scheduling analysis: software part
div.p: We design the software side of the analysis model by using the Software architecture and the Software Behavior MoSaRT diagrams (see Figure 6). To describe the behavior of a task in term of scheduling, each task in the architecture diagram must reference a task activity located in the software behavior diagram, where temporal parameters are defined (period, deadline, activation patterns, precedence relationships, etc.). We present on Fig. 6 properties of trigger and taskActivity.

On the Software Behavior diagram, only main relations between the tasks are represented such as Communication precedence shown between taskActivity9 and taskActivity8 (representing repectively tasks 9 and 8 of our example). We can notice that, the same relation is used between tasks 1 and 6: the nature of the communication is represented on the software architecture diagram as local resources or remote resources (instances of SoLocalCommResource or SoRemoteCommResource class). This modeling means that tasks send messages at the end of execution and the reception occurs at the beginning.

On the Software Architecture diagram, processes and the precedences (in terms on communication) between the tasks are defined. We present on the Figure 6 the properties related to a process (e.g. the tasks associated to the process), related to a task (e.g. the resources needed for the task), related to a remote communication resource (e.g. the path of a message through the Hp Flow Carrier set aspect). The property Hp Flow Carrier set is the sole aspect added in software diagrams, the majority of the extension resides in the hardware part.

div.head: B. Modeling oriented scheduling analysis: hardware part
div.p: The model gotten in software part can be mapped to different hardware architectures. We suppose that we have two architectures with different networks. The first architecture consists in a CAN network designed by MoSaRT as depicted in Figure 7. The messages priorities are indicated as an ordered list (of remote communication resources) that is among attributes CAN bus (instance of HpCommunicationChannel class).

In a LIN bus, the network is modeled through the transactions existing between the tasks with the software behavior diagram. Indeed, as the master requests or sends a message, there is a precedence between the tasks, the task sending or requesting a message always precedes the responding task.

The second hardware architecture, represented by Figure 8, is an AFDX network with 2 interconnected switches. Actually, the network can be changed to an AFDX one by adding switches on the communication channel as on Figure 8(a).
We also give on Figure 8(a) properties of new classes in the hardware part.

In this case, the remote communication resources of Figure 6 will play the role of virtual links. Thus, part (b) of Figure 8 shows the path of remoteCommResource_3 as a set of HpFlowCarrier instances (i.e. the links crossed by the virtual link).

div.head: C. Scheduling analysis via MoSaRT analysis repository
div.p: The second capability of the framework MoSaRT, which is the repository, analysis allows to help designers by guiding them to choose the appropriate test that matches their design. Indeed, this step is managed by a detection process based on a set of identification rules (rules that check the structure and behavior information contained in analysis models). Since this part of MoSaRT is out of the scope of this paper, we will not detail it (for more details, readers can see [7]). Applying the identification process to the analysis model that we get in sub-section V-B leads to the indication about the test and its accuracy as it is shown in Figure 9. The identification process presents the hypotheses verified by the system, the context's rules needed to apply the corresponding test, the references of the analysis presenting the rules of the context, and the characteristics of the proposed test. The holistic analysis test is implemented in different academic tools. MoSaRT provides a model transformation from models expressed in MoSaRT to input formalism of MAST.

div.head: D. Analysis results
div.p: We have considered that messages have Worst Case Transmission Times equal to 3ms.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have proposed a simple, but analyzable, meta-model for real-time networks. Our objective was to capitalize and to make explicit the analysis models instead of being implicit, ad-hoc and driven by analysts experiences. We have analyzed design features related the scheduling analysis of real-time networks by examining several tests. Then, we have extracted common concepts and specific concepts. These latter have been integrated in MoSaRT framework by extending the metamodel. This extension has taken advantage of MoSaRT and also model-driven engineering setting. As a result, the system can be designed incrementally by separating software and hardware layers. This mechanism has been stressed through the case study. We want to stress out the fact that the concepts proposed in this paper can also be included in several domain specific languages that need to offer network support. We are working on future extensions which consist in supporting the analysis of systems with cache memories. Also, we are working on the energy performance, in order to combine scheduling-aware and energy-aware analyses.
